name: Cross price elasticity
seoTitle: Cross price elasticity — Free Online Calculator
seoDesc: Cross price elasticity: work out price of product A (At time point 2) from the price of product A and the demand for product B. A free finance calculator…
summary: The Cross price elasticity calculator turns the price of product A, the demand for product B and the elasticity into price of product A (At time point 2). It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Cross price elasticity calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cross price elasticity calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports price of product A (At time point 2) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the price of product A (At time point 1), the demand for product B (At time point 1), the demand for product B (At time point 2) and the elasticity.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cross price elasticity calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Price of product A=price of product A × (elasticity × demand for product B + elasticity × demand for product B − demand for product B + demand for product B) ÷ (elasticity × demand for product B + elasticity × demand for product B + demand for product B − demand for product B)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Price of product A = 10, Demand for product B = 10 and Elasticity = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Price of product A = 10.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Price of product A = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Price of product A = 10 and Demand for product B = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cross price elasticity calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the price of product A, the demand for product B and the elasticity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Cross price elasticity calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns price of product A (At time point 2), derived from the price of product A, the demand for product B and the elasticity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cross price elasticity calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the price of product A, the demand for product B and the elasticity, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter price of product A (At time point 1) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Price of product A (At time point 1) opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Price of product A = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Cross price elasticity calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
